title: Rise of flowering plants
summary: Flowering plants' diversification rates increased through the early Cretaceous, and they rose to dominance in land floras towards the end of that period. Their true age is debated: estimates range from about 280 to 130 million years ago. Montsechia, an aquatic flowering plant from 130 to 125 million-year-old limestone in Spain, suggests water habitats may have mattered for some early lineages.

uncertainty.note: Dated by Early Cretaceous macrofossils including Montsechia vidalii (~130–125 Ma) and crown angiosperm fossil radiation records.

as_recorded.value: Barremian (130–125 million years ago) freshwater limestone in the Pyrenees and Iberian Range in Spain

where.modern_name: Serra del Montsec, Spanish Pyrenees (stand-in pin; flowering plants spread worldwide)
where.historical_name: Freshwater lacustrine basins on the Iberian microplate, western Tethys margin (no human political geography existed)

paleo.not_applicable: Global radiation of angiosperms beginning across Cretaceous continental and lacustrine ecosystems.

importance.justification: The rise and rapid radiation of flowering plants restructured terrestrial ecosystems, soil cycles, and pollinator coevolution, coming to dominate modern land vegetation.

related.because: The earlier colonization of land by non-vascular and seed plants provided the ancestral vascular flora and terrestrial soils from which angiosperms evolved.
The end-Cretaceous impact cleared gymnosperm canopies, accelerating the Cenozoic ecological dominance of modern angiosperm-dominated forests.
